description:
Hi everyone! We’re Haya Mahmoud and Zahra Hussain, third-year Software Engineering co-op students at the University of Guelph! 

We both love space, technology, and building creative projects that are fun and meaningful. We have experience in software development, programming, and working on real-world projects through our co-op experiences. We love brainstorming ideas, solving problems, and turning ambitious concepts into something people can actually use and enjoy!
summary:
Disastronauts is a fast-paced 3D browser game. It runs instantly at https://disastronauts.vercel.app/ with no download or account, on laptops, tablets and phones. Players run a small outpost in the real Jezero Crater on Mars and race three computer rivals to build the best colony in a 5-minute round. Each round lasts about five Mars days, called sols.

To answer the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge, we kept the game to three resources: Power, Life Support and Shielding. Every choice costs something. More crew need more Life Support, buildings use Power, and a bigger base needs more shielding. Dust storms, cold nights and solar flares test each plan, and Earth supply drops arrive after the real radio delay.

The game uses real NASA open data. Solar flares replay real events from DONKI, and an optional mode pulls the latest space weather live. Radiation levels come from Curiosity's RAD instrument, and the terrain comes from Mars Trek. Players also see Perseverance photos and NASA facts with their sources. An in-game screen shows which data is live and which is archived.

It's important because kids learn by making the same trade-offs real astronauts face, and losing a round is quick and doesn't punish them, so they want to play again.
details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

Disastronauts is a 3D browser game where kids aged 7–12 become astronauts running a small outpost in the real Jezero Crater on Mars. Each 5-minute round lasts about five Mars days (sols). Players walk their astronaut around the crater collecting supplies such as ice, broken solar panels, regolith (Mars soil) and supply crates. They bring these back to their lander, and the base grows automatically with new crew, shelters, solar panels, greenhouses and shield generators. Three computer rivals with different strategies (greedy, cautious and balanced) race to build their own colonies at the same time.

Players keep three bars healthy: Power, Life Support (air, water and food combined) and Shielding. Growth is never free. Every crew member uses Life Support, every building uses Power, and a bigger base needs more Shielding. Dust storms block the sun, cold nights drain Power for heating, and solar flares hurt any crew the shield doesn't cover. Players can call a supply drop from Earth, but it arrives only after the real Earth–Mars radio delay, so they have to plan ahead. The winner has the best Colony Score, which counts healthy crew, powered buildings, stored resources and mission stars. A small, well-run base beats a big base with sick crew and no power.

REAL NASA DATA

- Solar flares replay 181 real flares from NASA's DONKI space weather database. Each flare's class (C, M or X) sets its strength. An optional "Today's space weather" mode downloads the last 30 days of real flares and is labeled LIVE only if that download works.

- Radiation damage is based on Curiosity's RAD instrument readings from the Mars surface (NASA OSDR RadLab).

- The terrain is real Jezero Crater elevation (MOLA) with a CTX photo layer from NASA Mars Trek.

- Sol length, the 43% of Earth's sunlight that reaches Mars, and the 3–22 minute radio delay come from the NASA Mars Fact Sheet.

- Perseverance raw photos and cited NASA facts appear as rewards and pop-ups.

- An in-game "Real NASA Data" screen lists every dataset, what it changes in the game, whether it is live or archived, and the simplifications we made.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Kids learn by playing, not reading. They feel the same trade-offs real mission planners face: spending Power on the greenhouse or the shield, adding crew now or keeping enough Life Support for tonight, heading out for ice during a flare warning. Rounds are short, a loss still earns coins, and restarting takes one click, so failing becomes a way to learn rather than a punishment. Short glossary bubbles explain terms like sol, radiation and regolith in plain language. We want kids to come away curious about Mars, space weather and how NASA keeps astronauts safe, and to know that the data behind the game is real.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

- TypeScript, Three.js (3D graphics) and Vite (build tool)

- Vitest for automated tests of the game logic

- Python scripts to download and process NASA data (DONKI, OSDR RadLab, Mars Trek, Perseverance raw images)

- Web Audio API for sound effects generated in the browser

- Hosted on Vercel as a static website. It needs no server, accounts or tracking.

- Built with help from Claude Code, an AI coding assistant

- All 3D models, icons and UI are built in code from simple shapes, so no outside art files are needed.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

Instead of a quiz or simulator, we built a fast "grow to win" game in the style of popular kids' games, then made NASA data drive the rules. A real solar flare from May 2024 can decide whether your crew stays healthy. The map is a real crater you can explore on foot. Rival bases that lose all their crew turn into wrecks that other players can salvage, which teaches that every base depends on careful planning.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Age 7–12: only three resources, big icons, color-coded bars, one short sentence of text at a time, and a guided first-round tutorial

- Honesty with data: we never invented numbers. Every value is cited in the code and docs, archived data is never shown as live, and simplifications (such as flares seen from Earth being treated as hitting Mars) are explained in the game.

- Access: it plays in any browser with no download or account, works on phones and tablets with touch controls, and runs offline once loaded.

- Safety: earned coins only, with no real money, ads or data collection.

- Replayability: random spawns, different rival personalities and a different stretch of real flares each round
